phonemes.desc: Broad (velarized) bilabial nasal [m], before a; as in English 'mother', with the tongue already set for the wide vowel.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief; Old Irish stresses the first syllable throughout.
Voiceless velar fricative [x] — the rasp of Scottish 'loch' or German 'ach', never the hard k of 'cat'; lenited c, written ch, is a fricative in Old Irish.
Short open final [a], lightly sounded; two matching syllables, the second unstressed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAHKH-ah' — two short open a's, stress on the first, and let the ch rasp like the end of Scottish 'loch'. Modern Irish keeps the sound: Eamhain Mhacha is said with the same fricative.

kin.label: Old Irish
kin.form: Macha — the theonym and the woman's name are the same word; the texts know several bearers, all of whom the commentators treat as one goddess wearing several stories

kin.label: Proto-Celtic
kin.form: *magos, 'plain, field' — the root proposed for the name; Mag Macha, 'Macha's plain', is the country around Armagh (Matasović, EDPC)

kin.label: Gaulish cognate
kin.form: magos, 'plain, field' — the same word living in place-names such as Noviomagus and Caesaromagus, the continental witness to the root

kin.label: Modern Irish
kin.form: Macha — unbroken in Eamhain Mhacha (Navan Fort) and Ard Mhacha (Armagh), the county's own name

pronunciation.note: Macha is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the goddess's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: War, Sovereignty, Horses
domains.subtitle: The Woman Who Outran the King's Horses
domains.lead: Macha is the sovereignty figure of the Ulster Cycle: the otherworld woman who came to the door of the widower Cruinniuc and made his house prosper, and who — when her husband boasted at the assembly that she could outrun the king's horses — was brought out pregnant to the racetrack, outran the horses of Conchobar mac Nessa at the finish, gave birth to twins on the field, and laid on the men of Ulster the curse that shapes the whole Táin: in their hour of greatest need, the pangs of childbirth.

cards.name: The Race at the Assembly
cards.desc: Nine months gone, she begged for delay until she had given birth; the Ulaid refused. She raced the king's chariot-horses and beat them at the line.

cards.name: The Debility of the Ulaid
cards.desc: Her curse, the ces noínden: for five days and four nights, in every generation to the ninth, the men of Ulster would lie in the pangs of a woman in labor — whenever the province needed them most.

cards.name: Emain Macha
cards.desc: 'Macha's twins' — the boy and girl born at the finish line named the royal seat of Ulster, the Navan Fort that still stands outside Armagh.

cards.name: Macha Mongrúad
cards.desc: The red-maned queen of the Lebor Gabála who seized the kingship of Ireland in her own right and traced the rampart of Emain with the brooch of her neck.

symbols.name: The king's horses
symbols.meaning: Conchobar's unmatched chariot-pair — the boast that forced the race and the measure she outran

symbols.name: The twins
symbols.meaning: Emain, the boy and girl born on the racetrack — the naming of Ulster's royal seat and the price of its pride

symbols.name: The debility
symbols.meaning: Five days and four nights of a woman's labor-pangs, laid on a warrior people for nine generations — the curse that left Cú Chulainn to fight the Táin alone

symbols.name: The brooch of the queen
symbols.meaning: Macha Mongrúad marked the circuit of Emain with her eo-muin, her neck-brooch — sovereignty drawing the boundary of its own seat

symbols.name: Macha's mast
symbols.meaning: Mesrad Machae, 'Macha's crop' — the Táin's kenning for the severed heads of the slain, the war-goddess's harvest

mythology.lead: Macha's dossier is one great tale and a family of namesakes: the Debility of the Ulstermen gives her the race, the twins, and the curse; the Táin harvests the consequences; the Lebor Gabála remembers her as Nemed's wife and as the red-maned queen; and the genealogies fold her into the three of war beside [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]].

myths.title: The Woman at Cruinniuc's Door
myths.text:
Cruinniuc mac Agnomain was a rich farmer of the Ulaid, a widower with sons, and one day a woman he had never seen walked into his house, set about the work of it without a word, and lay with him that night. She stayed, and under her hand everything prospered — the house, the cattle, the table — and she told him the one condition of their life together: he must never speak of her, never boast of her. It is the old compact of the otherworld wife, and it held as long as he kept his mouth shut.

The tale that tells this — Noínden Ulad, 'The Debility of the Ulaid', one of the fore-tales of the Táin — is a sovereignty story before it is anything else: the land's own woman comes to the man of the land, and her condition is silence about the source of the plenty. Cruinniuc kept it until the day of the great assembly of the Ulaid, when the talk turned to the king's horses and there was nothing in the world faster.

myths.title: The Race, the Twins, and the Curse
myths.text:
At the assembly Cruinniuc forgot the condition and boasted: his wife could outrun the king's chariot-horses. Conchobar had him seized, and sent for the woman — who was nine months gone with twins. She begged the gathering for delay until she had given birth, 'for a mother bore each of you'; the Ulaid refused. She was set against the horses and raced them, and she beat them at the line — and at the line the pangs took her, and she was delivered of a boy and a girl on the field.

Then she cursed them: as she had been given no mercy in her labor, so the men of Ulster, in their hour of greatest straits, would suffer the pangs of a woman in childbirth — five days and four nights, for nine generations, every man save the boys and the women. And in most recensions she died there. The twins gave the royal seat of Ulster its name: Emain Macha, 'Macha's twins'. It is the most economical curse in Irish literature — one wrong, answered in exact kind, for nine generations.

myths.title: The Debility in the Táin
myths.text:
The curse is the engine of the greatest Irish epic. When [[medb|Medb]] of Connacht marches into Ulster for the Donn Cúailnge, the men of the province are down in the ces noínden, gripped by the pangs Macha laid on them — the curse spared the boys and the women, and it spared [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], who stands alone against the host of Ireland while the warriors of Emain writhe. The whole boyhood-deeds section of the Táin is narrated against the debility: one boy holding a province because a goddess was made to race in labor.

The Táin keeps her name in the language of battle as well. Its phrase for the harvest of heads is mesrad Machae, 'Macha's mast' — the crop the war-goddess gathers from the field. And the Lebor Gabála had already counted her among the three daughters of Ernmas: [[badb|Badb]] and Macha and Anand, 'of whom are the Paps of Anu' — the triple face of Irish war, the sisters the sources also gather under the one name [[morrigan|Morrígan]].

myths.title: The Queens and the Naming of Emain
myths.text:
The book of invasions remembers two earlier Machas. The first is Macha wife of Nemed, who came with the Nemedians in the days before the Túatha Dé Danann; she died in Ireland, and Ard Macha — Armagh, 'Macha's height' — and Mag Macha, 'Macha's plain', the country around it, are named from her grave.

The second is Macha Mongrúad, the red-maned daughter of Áed Rúad. When her father and his brothers Díthorba and Cimbáeth had held the kingship of Ireland in rotation, seven years each, and Áed died, the brothers refused the daughter her turn. She took it by war: she married Cimbáeth, defeated Díthorba's five sons — after going to them, the tale says, in the guise of a leprous hag — and held the kingship herself. It was she who marked out the rampart of Emain Macha with the brooch of her neck, her eo-muin, and made the captives dig it. The dindsenchas keeps both etymologies side by side — Macha's twins and Macha's brooch — and the tradition never chose between the goddess of the race and the queen of the fort.

lore.syncretism: Macha's clearest cross-border witness is Welsh, and it is the standard comparison of the handbooks: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, the otherworld woman on the horse no rider can overtake, who — falsely accused and shamed — is sentenced to sit at the horse-block and offer to carry guests on her back like a beast of burden. Mac Cana and Sjoestedt both set the two figures side by side: the sovereignty woman bound to horses, wronged by the men of the court, and made to bear an equine humiliation. Behind both stands the Gaulish horse-goddess Epona, whose altars run from Britain to the Danube — the one Celtic deity with a festival in the Roman calendar — the continental anchor of the comparison, cited as type, never as identity. Within the Irish corpus her structural kin are [[medb|Medb]], the sovereignty queen whose favor makes kings, and her own sisters of war, [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]], with whom the Lebor Gabála shares a mother.
lore.culturalLegacy: Macha rode the Celtic revival as the first wrong of the Ulster Cycle. Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) opens the epic with her — 'The Curse of Macha' — and made the race and the debility the gateway through which two generations of English readers entered the Táin. Thomas Kinsella's The Táin (1969) kept the fore-tale at the head of the epic, and the twinned figures of the wronged woman and the war-goddess have made Macha a standing subject in the study of Celtic sovereignty myth. On the ground, her names never went anywhere: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, one of the royal sites of Ireland and the ceremonial capital of Ulster, and Ard Macha — Armagh, the ecclesiastical primacy of Ireland, founded by Patrick in the fifth century — still carries her name in every address in the county. Modern scholarship from Mac Cana to Koch treats the race as the type-case of the Irish sovereignty goddess, and contemporary Celtic pagan practice honors her among the three of war.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Macha is the goddess of the exact answer. The Ulaid would not wait for her labor, so their labor is her labor: the pangs she suffered alone on the racetrack become the pangs of every fighting man in the province, whenever the province needs its men. Nothing in the curse is arbitrary; it is the wrong replayed on the body politic for nine generations, precise as a mirror. The Irish called it ces — the debility — and built their greatest epic inside it: a whole war fought by one boy because an assembly of men could not grant a pregnant woman a postponement.

Her name, if the etymologists are right, is simply 'field' — Mag Macha, Macha's plain, is the ground of Armagh itself. That is the sovereignty doctrine in a single word: the goddess is the land, the race is run on her, the fort is drawn by her brooch, and the men who rule there hold their strength on her sufferance. Macha asks the question every power eventually answers: what does it cost to use the land — and its women — as though they had no claims of their own?
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Macha — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: macha.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Macha is a textual goddess: no ogham stone names her, no votive inscription invokes her, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. Her manuscript witnesses are exact: Noínden Ulad survives in the Yellow Book of Lecan and its sister codices (Hull's edition in Celtica 8 rests on them), the Táin in its oldest recension in Lebor na hUidre, the Book of the Dun Cow (c. 1100), and the twelfth-century Book of Leinster, and the Lebor Gabála in the Book of Leinster and its companions. Her mythic address, by contrast, is one of the most instructive monuments in Atlantic Europe: Emain Macha is Navan Fort, Co. Armagh, where Waterman's excavations (1961–71) uncovered beneath the mound a forty-metre timber structure — a ring of great posts around a central oak — that dendrochronology dates to 95 BC, built in a single episode, filled with a stone cairn, burned, and buried under the mound still visible today. A building raised to be unmade is a ritual statement, not a residence; the standing interpretation, Lynn's, is a one-time ceremonial monument at the very seat the Ulster Cycle calls Macha's. No artifact names her; the identification of the fort with Emain Macha rests on the early medieval record, beginning with the annals and the Book of Armagh.
